# LLM Codebase Navigation & Understanding: What the Research Actually Shows

> **Status:** Archived query-layer note. See `docs/features/query-layer/README.md` for current docs and the local archive README for routing.

## TL;DR

- **No single technique dominates; the evidence favors a layered stack — precise symbol/graph navigation (LSP/SCIP-style or repo code graphs) + lexical+structural search as the backbone, with semantic embeddings as a supplement, and hierarchical localization on top — and several “obvious” additions (LLM-generated context files, pure vector RAG, very long context) measurably *hurt* or fail to beat simpler baselines.**
- **The strongest combination evidence is graph-augmented retrieval/localization**: RepoGraph (arXiv 2410.14684) gives an average 32.8% relative resolve-rate gain as a plug-in across four SWE-bench frameworks; LocAgent (arXiv 2503.09089) reaches 92.7% file-level localization; CGM (arXiv 2505.16901, NeurIPS 2025) hits 43.0% on SWE-bench Lite as the best open-weight-model method. All are BENCHMARK-grade, mostly Python/Java.
- **For your polyglot, multi-repo org, build on precise cross-repo code intelligence (SCIP/Glean-style indexes, which already cover TS/JS, Python, Go, Java, Rust, C/C++) rather than betting on embeddings or long-context.** Cross-repo is a genuinely distinct problem (different scaling, staleness, and dependency-resolution behavior) and merits a dedicated follow-up evaluation.

## Key Findings

1. **The “isolation vs combination” hypothesis holds: combinations win, but with diminishing returns and real interference.** Graph + retrieval + hierarchical localization is the most-validated stack. But adding context files, naive long-context, or pure semantic RAG often degrades results.
1. **Graph/structure-aware representations are the highest-leverage single addition** with ablation support (RepoGraph, LocAgent, CGM, RANGER). They beat pure embedding retrieval repeatedly.
1. **Agentic search (grep/glob/LSP tools, no pre-built index) is a serious, production-validated default** (Claude Code) that sidesteps staleness/security costs — at the price of tokens and latency.
1. **Two important negative results:** (a) LLM-generated AGENTS.md context files *reduce* task success and raise cost (ETH Zurich, arXiv 2602.11988); (b) Agentless (arXiv 2407.01489) showed simple hierarchical localization beat complex agents on SWE-bench Lite at a fraction of the cost.
1. **Long context does not replace retrieval/navigation** and can hurt even with perfect retrieval (arXiv 2510.05381).
1. **Language skew is real and consequential:** most evidence is Python/Java; TypeScript is a consistent weak spot; statically-typed/build-coupled languages behave differently, though some techniques generalize.

-----

## Tier 1 — Strong ablation or deployed evidence

<technique name="Repository code graph as plug-in context (RepoGraph)" family="code graphs & traversal" maturity="established">
<summary>A line-level repository graph (nodes = lines defining/referencing symbols; edges = def/ref dependencies) from which ego-graphs are retrieved and injected into procedural or agent frameworks.</summary>
<how_it_works>Parses the repo via tree-sitter-style code-line parsing into a graph encoding definitions and references. Sub-graph retrieval extracts k-hop ego-graphs around keywords; these are flattened and appended to prompts (procedural) or exposed as a search_repograph action (agent).</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="strong" type="benchmark">arXiv 2410.14684 (ICLR 2025). Integrated as a plug-in into four frameworks (Agentless, SWE-agent, AutoCodeRover, and others) on SWE-bench Lite, yielding an average 32.8% relative improvement in success rate. Also tested on CrossCodeEval to show transfer to repo-level completion. Open-source artifact released with cached graphs for SWE-bench repos.</evidence>
<isolation>As a standalone retrieval substitute it outperforms semantic-similarity retrieval that ignores true dependencies; the paper frames it as a complement, not a full agent.</isolation>
<in_combination>Its central result IS a combination study: graph context plugged into both procedural (Agentless) and agentic (SWE-agent, AutoCodeRover) pipelines. Gains are consistent across all four, evidence of synergy with existing localization/repair stacks rather than interference.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Demonstrated at single-repo scale. Line-level graph construction "may take a long time to run for a repo," suggesting scaling friction at org scale; no cross-repo evaluation.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Graph build is non-trivial per repo (hence the cached version they ship); no incremental-update study.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Graph-guided localization agent (LocAgent)" family="code graphs & traversal + agentic navigation" maturity="established">
<summary>Parses a codebase into a directed heterogeneous graph (files, classes, functions; edges for imports, invocations, inheritance) and lets an LLM agent traverse it with multi-hop reasoning to localize where changes are needed.</summary>
<how_it_works>Builds a lightweight graph index capturing structure + dependencies, then exposes traversal tools (definition lookup, tracing call stacks) to an agent that performs coarse-to-fine localization without loading the full repo into context.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="strong" type="benchmark">arXiv 2503.09089 (ACL 2025). Up to 92.7% file-level localization accuracy. A fine-tuned Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B matches SOTA proprietary models at ~86% lower cost; improves downstream GitHub issue resolution by 12% (Pass@10). Open-source (gersteinlab/LocAgent).</evidence>
<isolation>Strong on the localization sub-task in isolation; the graph representation is the core contribution.</isolation>
<in_combination>Compares graph-agent localization vs Agentless's hierarchical prompting; the graph approach wins on precision and recall. Difficulty analysis by graph "hop distance" shows the multi-hop graph traversal is what helps on harder, more distant dependencies.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Single-repo; the heterogeneous-graph approach is in principle extensible across repos but not evaluated there.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>"Lightweight" index; no incremental/staleness study reported.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Graph-integrated LLM (Code Graph Model, CGM)" family="neuro-symbolic / learned graph representation" maturity="emerging">
<summary>Integrates a repository code graph directly into an LLM via graph-aware attention masking, rather than just retrieving text into the prompt.</summary>
<how_it_works>Repository represented as a directed graph with 7 node types (REPO→PACKAGE→FILE→CLASS→FUNCTION granularity) and edges for hierarchical "contains" plus reference dependencies (calls/imports/extends). Node text is encoded by a CodeT5+ encoder, projected via an MLP adapter into the LLM input space, and the causal attention mask is replaced by a graph-aware mask derived from the adjacency matrix (GNN-like message passing). Trained with LoRA on Qwen2.5-72B via subgraph reconstruction pre-training + noisy fine-tuning. A 4-module Graph RAG pipeline (Rewriter→Retriever→Reranker→Reader) replaces Agentless's 10 steps.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="strong" type="benchmark">arXiv 2505.16901 (NeurIPS 2025). CGM-SWE-PY on Qwen2.5-72B: 43.0% on SWE-bench Lite (1st among open-weight-model methods; beat Moatless+DeepSeek-V3 at 30.67% by 12.33 points), 50.4% on SWE-bench Verified. CGM-Multi: 14.29% on SWE-bench-java Verified (1st). Open-source (codefuse-ai/CodeFuse-CGM); later released checkpoints (V1.2, Jan 2025) report up to 44.0% on Lite — distinct from the paper's 43.0%.</evidence>
<isolation>The graph-integrated model is the unit of evaluation; ablations (§5.3/App C.7) state the graph-aware attention mask is "essential" and the subgraph-reconstruction pre-training "significantly contributes," though exact numeric deltas live in the appendix and were not extracted here.</isolation>
<in_combination>Combines learned graph encoding + Graph RAG retrieval + reranking; the reranker is called "pivotal." Joint fine-tuning of encoder+adapter+decoder beats freezing any component.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Trained/evaluated per-repo (Python, Java). No cross-repo evaluation; the heavyweight training pipeline is a barrier to org-scale adoption.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Requires graph construction + model fine-tuning; no incremental indexing story. Heaviest build cost of the Tier 1 methods.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Hierarchical coarse-to-fine localization (Agentless)" family="iterative/hierarchical localization" maturity="established">
<summary>A non-agentic, fixed three-phase pipeline: hierarchical localization (file → class/function → edit location), repair via sampled diffs, and patch validation — deliberately avoiding autonomous agent decision-making.</summary>
<how_it_works>Uses LLM prompting + embedding-based retrieval to narrow from suspicious files to fine-grained edit locations, then samples multiple candidate patches in diff format, filters with regression/reproduction tests, and re-ranks via majority voting.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="strong" type="benchmark">arXiv 2407.01489 (Xia et al. 2024). Best open-source approach on SWE-bench Lite at release: 82 fixes (27.3%) on GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) at an average $0.34 per issue — versus roughly $3.34 per issue for some agent approaches; a later configuration reached 32.00% (96 fixes). This is the canonical "simplicity beats complexity" result.</evidence>
<isolation>Hierarchical localization alone is highly competitive; the key finding is that a simple, interpretable pipeline matched or beat complex agents.</isolation>
<in_combination>Serves as the substrate other techniques plug into (RepoGraph adds graph context at each step; Nemotron-CORTEXA replaces its prompt-based localization with a structure-augmented agent and reports higher precision/recall on SWE-bench Verified).</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Single-repo issue resolution; no cross-repo dimension.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>No persistent index; recomputed per task, so no staleness — at the cost of repeated per-task compute.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Agentic search (grep/glob/LSP, no pre-built index)" family="agentic exploration / tool-use navigation" maturity="established">
<summary>The agent explores the live codebase with filesystem and search tools (ripgrep, glob, read, and optionally LSP) on demand, instead of pre-retrieving from an index.</summary>
<how_it_works>The LLM issues exact-match searches and file reads, refines iteratively, and reasons over results within its context window. No embeddings, vector DB, or index to maintain.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="moderate" type="deployed">Production-validated in Claude Code. Anthropic removed its early Voyage-embedding vector-RAG path in favor of agentic search; on the Latent Space podcast (May 2025), Claude Code creator Boris Cherny said: "originally… very early versions of Claude actually used RAG… we were just using Voyage… Eventually, we landed on just agentic search… it outperformed everything. By a lot. And this was surprising… This was just vibes, so internal vibes. There's some internal benchmarks also, but mostly vibes." Treat the magnitude as DEPLOYED/ANECDOTAL, not independently benchmarked. Cursor, Devin, and Gemini CLI converge on similar grep-first strategies. [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200&%3D%3D "MindStudio")](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/is-rag-dead-what-ai-agents-use-instead) Sourcegraph's CodeScaleBench found agents overwhelmingly prefer exact keyword search even when semantic tools are offered (4,813 keyword vs 587 NL-search calls).</evidence>
<isolation>Strong default for code navigation; exact matching is precise, always fresh, and zero-setup. Critics (Milvus) note it burns tokens and misses conceptual/semantic queries.</isolation>
<in_combination>Best results reported when combined with precise navigation (LSP/SCIP) and, for concept queries, a semantic index as fallback — the emerging "hybrid" consensus. Cursor uses tree-sitter + filesystem search as primary, embeddings as a supplementary layer. [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200&%3D%3D "MindStudio")](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/is-rag-dead-what-ai-coding-agents-use-instead)</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Pure local agentic search does not scale across many repos without a federated search/index layer (this is exactly the gap Sourcegraph MCP fills).</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Best-in-class: nothing to index, no staleness, no index security exposure. Cost is paid per-query in tokens/latency.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Precise symbol indexes (LSP / LSIF / SCIP) and org-scale code graphs (Glean)" family="symbol indexes / cross-repo intelligence" maturity="established">
<summary>Compiler-accurate indexes of definitions, references, implementations, and types, queryable for precise navigation across repository boundaries.</summary>
<how_it_works>Language-specific indexers (scip-typescript, scip-python, scip-java, scip-clang, rust-analyzer) emit a language-agnostic index (SCIP, successor to LSIF). Symbols get unique IDs including package+version, enabling version-aware cross-repo "go to definition / find references." Meta's Glean stores typed facts in a Datalog-queryable DB (Angle) and supports incremental indexing of monorepos with billions of facts. [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200& "Glean")](https://glean.software/)</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="strong" type="deployed">Deployed at Sourcegraph and Meta. SCIP indexers cover the exact polyglot set in scope: TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Java/Scala/Kotlin, Go, Rust, C/C++ (scip-clang), C#, Ruby, PHP. [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200& "Glean")](https://glean.software/) Per Sourcegraph's scip-typescript announcement: "When we migrated from lsif-node to scip-typescript in the Sourcegraph codebase, the indexing job in our CI went from ~40 minutes (12 parallel jobs) down to ~5 minutes (1 job)." scip-clang indexes are ~10–20% the size of LSIF. Glean is open-source (facebookincubator/Glean) and powers code browsing/search/doc-gen at Meta. [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200&%3D%3D "FB")](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/12/19/developer-tools/glean-open-source-code-indexing/)</evidence>
<isolation>Gold standard for precision navigation; complements rather than competes with LLM reasoning. Used directly by coding agents and IDEs when accuracy and cross-file/cross-language reasoning matter. [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200& "Glean")](https://glean.software/)</isolation>
<in_combination>Increasingly exposed to agents via MCP (Sourcegraph MCP: go_to_definition, find_references, search). [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200& "Sourcegraph")](https://sourcegraph.com/mcp) Reported ~4,000 tokens for cross-repo understanding vs ~48,000 tokens for grep-and-read equivalent [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200&%3D%3D "Medium")](https://medium.com/@ajaynz/getting-the-most-out-of-coding-agents-with-sourcegraph-mcp-ded895d41d18) — a strong token-economics argument for precise indexes as an agent backend (vendor-reported).</in_combination>
<cross_repo>This is the cross-repo workhorse. SCIP resolves symbols across repositories via version-aware lookups; falls back to search-based nav when an index is missing for a file/version. Cross-repo precision requires indexes for BOTH dependent and dependency at compatible versions.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Glean supports incremental indexing (index changes in O(changes) not O(repository); [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200&%3D%3D "Glean")](https://glean.software/blog/incremental/) ownership-set tracking adds ~7% DB size). [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200&%3D%3D "Glean")](https://glean.software/blog/incremental/) Build-system coupling (Bazel) needed for fast incrementality in C/C++; scip-clang incrementality was a known gap. SCIP indexes must be periodically regenerated; staleness triggers search-based fallback.</maintainability>
</technique>

-----

## Tier 2 — Solid benchmark evidence

<technique name="Iterative retrieve-then-generate (RepoCoder)" family="iterative retrieve-generate" maturity="established">
<summary>Alternates a similarity-based retriever with a code LM, using the model's own draft completion to refine the next retrieval query.</summary>
<how_it_works>Round 1 retrieves by similarity to the in-file context; the generated completion is fed back to retrieve more relevant snippets; repeat. Bridges the gap between retrieval context and intended completion.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="strong" type="benchmark">arXiv 2303.12570 (EMNLP 2023). Improves in-file completion baseline by >10% across line/API/function-body completion and consistently beats vanilla RAG on the RepoEval benchmark (introduced in the same paper).</evidence>
<isolation>Strong single-technique gain over both no-retrieval and one-shot RAG baselines.</isolation>
<in_combination>The iteration itself is the combination (retrieval ⊗ generation); demonstrates synergy between drafting and retrieval. Foundational for later hybrid systems.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Designed for single-repo completion; retrieval scope is the current repo.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Re-retrieval each iteration adds latency/token cost; no persistent index maintenance studied.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Ranked repository map (Aider repo map; PageRank over symbol graph)" family="repository maps" maturity="established">
<summary>A token-budgeted structural summary of the whole repo: tree-sitter extracts symbol defs/refs, a graph of files is built, and personalized PageRank ranks the most important symbols to include.</summary>
<how_it_works>Tree-sitter tags (def/ref) form a directed multigraph (files as nodes; edges weighted 10× for mentioned/well-named identifiers, 50× for chat files, 0.1× for private). PageRank with a personalization vector biased to the active conversation ranks symbols; a binary search fits the top-ranked definitions into a token budget (default 1k). Rebuilt before each LLM call.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="moderate" type="deployed">Deployed in Aider. Aider's own benchmarks indicate PageRank-scored context yields higher edit accuracy than naive file inclusion — DEPLOYED but vendor-reported, not independently ablated. Supports 130+ languages via tree-sitter; falls back to Pygments for reference extraction in languages where tree-sitter gives only defs (e.g., C++).</evidence>
<isolation>Effective context-selection heuristic that beats "send the mentioned files"; graph-based relevance is the core idea.</isolation>
<in_combination>Designed to work alongside semantic search and explicit @-references; complementary to agentic file reads.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Single-repo by construction; the map is the git repo.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Tag cache invalidated by mtime; rebuilt cheaply per call. Good incremental behavior at single-repo scale.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Graph-enhanced retrieval agent (RANGER)" family="code graphs + hybrid retrieval" maturity="emerging">
<summary>Builds a persistent repository knowledge graph (down to variable level) with text descriptions + embeddings on nodes, then serves both entity queries (Cypher lookups) and NL queries (MCTS-guided graph traversal with cross-encoder reranking).</summary>
<how_it_works>AST parsing builds the graph; nodes augmented with embeddings to bridge code↔NL. [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200&%3D "arXiv")](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.25257) Entity queries → fast Cypher; NL queries → Monte Carlo Tree Search traversal where a bi-encoder expands promising paths and an expensive cross-encoder scores only high-value candidates. [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200&%3D "ResearchGate")](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/396048813_RANGER_--_Repository-Level_Agent_for_Graph-Enhanced_Retrieval)</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="strong" type="benchmark">arXiv 2509.25257 (Sep 2025). Beats Qwen3-8B-embedding retrieval on CodeSearchNet and RepoQA (NDCG@10/Recall@10); [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200&%3D "ResearchGate")](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/396048813_RANGER_--_Repository-Level_Agent_for_Graph-Enhanced_Retrieval) superior cross-file dependency retrieval on RepoBench (Accuracy@5 up to 0.5471); [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200& "Emergent Mind")](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/repobench) RANGER+BM25 gives the highest exact-match on CrossCodeEval Python split (471 repos). [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200& "arXiv")](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.25257v1) Explicit finding: "Pure semantic retrieval performs poorly which supports the need for cross-file graph traversal over linear index search." [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200& "arXiv")](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.25257v1)</evidence>
<isolation>Graph traversal alone beats strong embedding baselines on retrieval metrics.</isolation>
<in_combination>Best result is RANGER+BM25 (graph ⊗ lexical) — direct evidence that hybrid lexical+structural beats either alone. Cross-encoder reranking on top of bi-encoder expansion is another working combination.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Per-repo knowledge graph; persistent graph is a step toward org scale but not evaluated cross-repo.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Persistent graph (vs per-query rebuild) is a maintainability plus; MCTS + cross-encoder add query cost. Authors note repeated high-fidelity LLM scoring (in MCTS-based peers like LingmaAgent) is expensive and nondeterministic. [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200&%3D "arXiv")](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.25257)</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Hybrid lexical + semantic retrieval" family="semantic/embedding + lexical search" maturity="established">
<summary>Combines exact lexical matching (BM25/grep) with dense embedding retrieval to cover both symbol-precise and concept-level queries.</summary>
<how_it_works>Lexical handles identifiers, error strings, and exact symbols; semantic handles paraphrased/conceptual queries. Results are merged/reranked.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="moderate" type="benchmark">CrossCodeEval (arXiv 2310.11248) shows retrieval roughly doubles-to-triples exact match over in-file-only (e.g., CodeGen 7.7%→14.5% with BM25 on Python), but even oracle retrieval keeps EM <23% — retrieval helps but is far from solved. CodeRAG-Bench (arXiv 2406.14497) finds retrieval most benefits weaker models and that retrieval quality, chunking, and document count materially change outcomes. RANGER+BM25 result (above) is direct hybrid evidence.</evidence>
<isolation>Pure semantic/embedding retrieval underperforms on code: embeddings capture fuzzy similarity that often isn't meaningful for code; [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200&%3D%3D "Threads")](https://www.threads.com/@carnage4life/post/DVWi8P-kkkB/anthropic-replacing-rag-with-grep-for-claude-is-fascinating-and-the-rationale) multiple sources report grep beating embeddings for symbol-precise tasks.</isolation>
<in_combination>Hybrid is the emerging best practice; semantic alone is dominated by lexical+structural for navigation. Sweet spot is structural/lexical as backbone + semantic as fallback for concept queries and huge repos.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Embedding index scales across repos but inherits staleness, re-embedding cost, and security exposure of a stored representation of proprietary code.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Vector index needs continuous re-embedding as files change ("the indexing tax"); incremental sync (e.g., Merkle-tree-based, as in Cursor) mitigates but adds engineering.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Data-flow-aware pretrained representation (GraphCodeBERT)" family="learned representation / AST+dataflow" maturity="established">
<summary>A pretrained code model that incorporates data-flow (variable def-use relations) into the representation rather than treating code as a token sequence.</summary>
<how_it_works>Augments masked-LM pretraining with data-flow edges (where-the-value-comes-from), giving a structure-aware code embedding used for search, clone detection, and refinement.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="moderate" type="benchmark">Foundational (2021) representation that underpins later structure-aware retrieval; widely cited as a backbone. Included here because it established that data-flow structure improves code representation over sequence-only models; superseded for many tasks by larger code LMs.</evidence>
<isolation>Demonstrated gains on code search and clone detection vs CodeBERT at the time.</isolation>
<in_combination>Used as an embedding component inside larger retrieval pipelines.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Representation-level; cross-repo applicability depends on the surrounding retrieval system.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Static pretrained model; embeddings need recomputation as code changes.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Code-use over tool-use agent (CodeNav)" family="agentic exploration" maturity="emerging">
<summary>An agent that automatically indexes and searches code blocks in a target codebase, imports relevant snippets, and iterates with execution feedback — instead of requiring manual tool registration.</summary>
<how_it_works>Indexes code blocks (Elasticsearch backend), searches for relevant snippets given a query, imports/uses them, and refines via execution feedback over multiple turns.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="moderate" type="benchmark">arXiv 2406.12276 (Allen Institute for AI). Quantitatively compares "code-use" (only target codebase) vs "tool-use" (privileged tool descriptions) across three benchmarks; studies the value of seeing source code vs NL descriptions. Open-source (allenai/codenav). Authors note evaluation was on relatively small codebases (scalability is acknowledged future work).</evidence>
<isolation>Shows agents can use a codebase directly without pre-registered tools — a representation/navigation finding.</isolation>
<in_combination>Ablates the effect of different tool/library descriptions on code-use performance.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Not evaluated at scale; acknowledged limitation.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Requires a running Elasticsearch index; staleness not studied.</maintainability>
</technique>

-----

## Tier 3 — Promising / emerging, weaker evidence

<technique name="Code Property Graph + LLM (neuro-symbolic, LLMxCPG / MoCQ)" family="neuro-symbolic / code property graph" maturity="emerging">
<summary>Combines classic CPGs (AST + control-flow + data-flow, à la Joern/CodeQL) with LLMs — either using the LLM to generate graph queries, or using CPG slices to feed the LLM a minimal vulnerability-relevant context.</summary>
<how_it_works>LLMxCPG: an LLM generates CPG queries to extract a minimal code slice (reducing code size 67.84–90.93%), then a second LLM classifies it. MoCQ: an LLM auto-generates end-to-end vulnerability detection patterns (sources, sinks, control-flow, sanitizers) for a symbolic engine.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="moderate" type="benchmark">LLMxCPG (arXiv 2507.16585, USENIX Security 2025): 15–40% F1 improvement over SOTA on verified vulnerability datasets; robust to syntactic modifications; handles multi-function/whole-project slices. MoCQ (arXiv 2504.16057): neuro-symbolic vulnerability detection for C/C++/web languages.</evidence>
<isolation>The CPG slice is what enables multi-function reasoning the LLM couldn't do on raw tokens.</isolation>
<in_combination>Direct neuro-symbolic combination: symbolic CPG for precision + LLM for semantics/pattern synthesis. Relevant to change-impact and security navigation.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>CPGs are typically per-project; interprocedural across repos is hard (KNighter explicitly lacked interprocedural analysis). Whole-project slices are demonstrated.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>CPG construction (Joern-style) is build-aware and can be heavy; no incremental study.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Agentic memory over codebases (persistent/experience memory)" family="agentic memory" maturity="experimental">
<summary>Persistent memory layers that store code-state checkpoints, prior task trajectories, or reusable "experience" across agent sessions.</summary>
<how_it_works>Architectures range from working-memory code-state checkpoints (SWE-Adept), hierarchical memory (Confucius Code Agent), to episodic+semantic repair memory (ExpeRepair) and experience reuse pools (SWE-ContextBench).</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="weak" type="benchmark">Mixed and early. ExpeRepair (2025) ablates dual memory on SWE-bench Lite and finds both episodic+semantic components help. SWE-ContextBench (2026) finds oracle-provided experience summaries improve resolution ~8 points BUT autonomous reuse without reliable selection can DEGRADE performance. GitHub Copilot reported a 7-point PR-merge increase with agentic memory in a Jan 2026 A/B test (DEPLOYED but not reproducible). A controlled benchmark reported 15–28% token savings.</evidence>
<isolation>Memory helps only when retrieval/selection of the right memory is reliable; otherwise neutral-to-harmful.</isolation>
<in_combination>Best paired with reliable selection (oracle-guided). This mirrors the AGENTS.md finding: correctly-scoped context helps, broadly-applied context hurts.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Conceptually strong for org-scale reuse but unproven; most memory systems benchmark on conversational recall, not code.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Memory staleness/curation is itself an open problem.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Steering / context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules)" family="steering / rules files" maturity="established (practice), weak (evidence)">
<summary>Repo-level Markdown files giving agents project structure, tooling, conventions, and constraints.</summary>
<how_it_works>Read by the agent before/at task start (Claude builds a referenced-file chain; Codex front-loads from the full hierarchy). Can be per-directory layered.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="moderate" type="benchmark">The first rigorous study is a NEGATIVE result: ETH Zurich/LogicStar "Evaluating AGENTS.md" (arXiv 2602.11988, Feb 2026), using a new AGENTBENCH (138 tasks from 12 niche repos with developer-written context files) plus SWE-bench Lite. Findings: LLM-generated context files DECREASE success ~3% on average; developer-written files improve only ~4%; both increase inference cost >20% by encouraging more exploration/testing. Directory overviews specifically did not help agents find files faster. A descriptive study of 2,303 context files (arXiv 2511.12884) and one of 2,926 repos exist but do not measure task success.</evidence>
<isolation>On its own, the LLM-generated variety is net-negative; minimal human-written tooling notes are marginally positive.</isolation>
<in_combination>Acts as a "compensation mechanism for missing documentation, not a performance booster on top of good docs." Recommendation from the evidence: keep minimal, human-written, requirement-focused; avoid auto-generated /init files.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Per-repo; per-directory layering untested empirically beyond the negative directory-overview finding.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Files go stale ("burst-then-taper" maintenance pattern observed); maintenance burden with unclear payoff.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Long-context (whole-repo-in-context) as alternative to retrieval" family="long-context vs retrieval" maturity="emerging">
<summary>Feeding very large portions of a repo directly into a long-context window instead of retrieving.</summary>
<how_it_works>Relies on 200K–10M token windows to hold repo content; the model attends over everything.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="strong" type="benchmark">Consistently dominated by retrieval on cost and often accuracy. "Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval" (arXiv 2510.05381) shows distractor volume degrades reasoning even with perfect retrieval. Repo-QA work (arXiv 2603.26567) notes longer input reduces ability to capture cross-context dependencies and that source-code relationships aren't linear. "Retrieval meets Long Context" shows 4K+retrieval ≈ 16K long-context at lower compute.</evidence>
<isolation>Net-negative beyond moderate lengths; "lost in the middle" and attention dilution. Useful only for moderate, static, self-contained contexts.</isolation>
<in_combination>Best as retrieval + moderate context, not replacement. Long context does not obviate navigation.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Infeasible to hold an org's code in context; retrieval/navigation is mandatory at scale.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>No index, but per-query token cost is extreme and grows with repo size.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="Git-derived historical context (churn, co-change, blame, ownership)" family="historical / git-derived context" maturity="experimental">
<summary>Using version-control signals — co-change coupling, churn, blame, ownership — to inform which files are relevant or risky.</summary>
<how_it_works>Mines commit history for files that change together (logical coupling), high-churn hotspots, and ownership to prioritize navigation/impact analysis.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="weak" type="anecdotal">Well-established in classic mining-software-repositories research as predictive of change impact, but I found little rigorous evaluation of it as an LLM-navigation signal in the 2024–2026 agent literature. Glean ingests cross-system links (code↔docs↔incidents); [![](claude-citation:/icon.png?validation=CBA0D9BD-CC72-4F63-8FC7-ADF6A628E200&%3D%3D "Glean")](https://docs.glean.com/security/how-code-search-works) Sourcegraph indexes commit history (Context Lineage). Treat LLM-specific effectiveness as UNVERIFIED.</evidence>
<isolation>Plausible but unproven as a standalone LLM-navigation signal.</isolation>
<in_combination>Likely complementary to graph/symbol navigation for change-impact; no ablation found.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Co-change across repos is weak unless commits are coordinated (monorepo favors this).</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Cheap to compute incrementally from git; naturally current.</maintainability>
</technique>

<technique name="UML / architecture recovery and diagrammatic representations" family="architecture recovery" maturity="experimental">
<summary>Recovering higher-level architecture (module/component diagrams, UML) as a navigation/comprehension aid.</summary>
<how_it_works>Static analysis or LLM summarization produces component/dependency diagrams summarizing system structure.</how_it_works>
<evidence strength="weak" type="anecdotal">I found no strong 2024–2026 benchmark evidence that recovered UML/architecture diagrams improve LLM navigation/localization specifically. Repo maps (Aider) and dependency graphs are the practical realization of this idea with evidence; classical UML recovery for LLM agents is UNVERIFIED here.</evidence>
<isolation>Unproven for LLM navigation.</isolation>
<in_combination>Conceptually subsumed by repo maps / code graphs, which have evidence.</in_combination>
<cross_repo>Architecture views could help org-scale comprehension but unevaluated.</cross_repo>
<maintainability>Recovered diagrams go stale; regeneration cost.</maintainability>
</technique>

-----

## <combination_findings>

The literature directly supports the working hypothesis that **a combination dominates, but the optimal stack is “precise structure first, semantics as supplement,” not “everything on.”**

1. **Graph/structure ⊗ retrieval ⊗ hierarchical localization is the best-validated stack.** RepoGraph’s headline result is a *combination* study (graph context plugged into four frameworks; +32.8% avg relative). LocAgent beats Agentless’s hierarchical prompting specifically by adding graph traversal. CGM stacks learned graph encoding + Graph RAG + reranking. RANGER’s best number is RANGER+BM25 (graph ⊗ lexical), and it explicitly reports pure semantic retrieval underperforming graph traversal.
1. **Hybrid lexical+semantic beats either alone, but lexical/structural is the backbone.** Across CrossCodeEval, CodeRAG-Bench, RANGER, and the production testimony of Claude Code/Cursor/Sourcegraph, exact/structural matching is the workhorse and embeddings are a fallback for conceptual queries. Agents empirically *prefer* keyword search even when given semantic tools (CodeScaleBench: 4,813 keyword vs 587 NL calls). 
1. **Precise symbol intelligence (SCIP/Glean) as an agent backend is the strongest cross-repo combination signal**, with a concrete token-economics case (~4K vs ~48K tokens for cross-repo understanding)  — though that figure is Sourcegraph-reported (DEPLOYED, vendor).
1. **Diminishing returns / interference are real.** Adding context files, naive long context, or autonomous (unselective) memory degrades or fails to beat simpler baselines. The recurring principle: *correctly-scoped, reliably-relevant context helps; broadly-assembled, autonomously-applied context hurts* (the AGENTS.md and SWE-ContextBench findings converge on this).

**Bottom line for an optimal stack:** precise symbol/graph navigation + lexical search as the backbone; iterative retrieve-generate or hierarchical localization for the task loop; semantic embeddings only as a concept-query fallback; agentic exploration to glue it together. Heavyweight learned-graph models (CGM) and CPG neuro-symbolic methods are high-value for specific tasks (localization, vuln detection) but carry the largest build/maintenance cost.

## <negative_results>

- **LLM-generated context files reduce success and raise cost** (arXiv 2602.11988): −3% avg for LLM-generated, only +4% for human-written, +20% cost; directory overviews specifically don’t speed up file-finding. Strongest single negative result for the steering-files family.
- **Complex agents did not beat simple hierarchical localization** (Agentless, arXiv 2407.01489) on SWE-bench Lite, at roughly one-tenth the per-issue cost ($0.34 vs ~$3.34) — the canonical “complexity didn’t pay” result that reset SWE-agent baselines.
- **Long context does not beat retrieval and can hurt even with perfect retrieval** (arXiv 2510.05381; arXiv 2603.26567).
- **Pure semantic/embedding retrieval underperforms** lexical/structural for code navigation (RANGER’s explicit finding; Claude Code’s RAG→agentic-search reversal).
- **Autonomous memory reuse without reliable selection degrades performance** (SWE-ContextBench, 2026); memory helps only with reliable (oracle-like) selection.
- **Benchmark caveat:** SWE-bench Lite/Verified are near-saturated and partially memorizable; the AGENTS.md authors built AGENTBENCH precisely because popular repos may be in training data. Treat single-benchmark SWE-bench deltas with caution.

## <cross_repo_assessment>

Cross-repo is a **genuinely distinct problem** and the evidence base is much thinner than single-repo:

- **What changes:** dependency resolution must cross repo boundaries (SCIP needs version-aware indexes for *both* sides; missing indexes silently degrade to text search). Monorepos favor incremental indexing and co-change signals; polyrepos fragment the graph and complicate version matching. Token economics shift decisively toward precise indexes over grep-and-read at scale.
- **What exists:** SCIP/LSIF (Sourcegraph) and Glean (Meta) are the deployed cross-repo/org-scale systems, both covering your full language set. CodeScaleBench (Sourcegraph, 370 tasks across 40+ repos including Kubernetes/Django/Linux/VSCode and 9 languages, split into 150 SDLC + 220 Org tasks) is the most relevant multi-repo agent benchmark. It reports MCP-augmented agents were ~30% cheaper, ~38% faster, and 2–3× better on retrieval precision, with a dramatic org-scale cross-repo lift (baseline precision@5 ≈ 0.007 vs MCP ≈ 0.471). **There is a reported inconsistency to flag:** Sourcegraph’s narrative reports security/incident-debugging *gains* under MCP (security ~+10.6%, incident debugging ~+11.2%) on one suite, while the same blog’s per-task-type SDLC reward table shows MCP *improving* understand (+0.115), refactor (+0.103), and fix (+0.099) but *reducing* secure (−0.050) and debug (−0.037). The likeliest reconciliation is that these are different task suites/metrics (Org vs SDLC; precision vs reward), but it means even precise cross-repo retrieval is **not uniformly positive across task types** — treat the vendor’s aggregate gains cautiously. CrossCodeEval and DependEval cover cross-file (within-repo) dependency reasoning; DependEval explicitly finds LLMs struggle with directory structure, cross-file edits, and statically-typed languages.
- **Recommendation: YES — commission a dedicated cross-repo follow-up.** The single-repo literature does not transfer cleanly. Scope it around (a) precise index coverage and incrementality for your statically-typed/build-coupled languages (Go/Rust/C/C++ via Bazel-aware indexing), (b) version-aware cross-repo symbol resolution, and (c) a CodeScaleBench-style internal eval on your own repos to measure token economics and per-task-type lift (so you can detect the secure/debug interference above on your own workloads).

## <gaps>

- **No head-to-head ablation of the full proposed stack.** The literature evaluates 2–4-technique hybrids; nobody has ablated “graph + lexical + semantic + hierarchical + memory” jointly on one benchmark. The optimal-stack claim is an inference across studies, not a single controlled result.
- **Language generalization is under-measured.** Most ablations are Python (SWE-bench, RepoEval) or Python/Java. TypeScript is a consistent weak spot: on CrossCodeEval, StarCoder2’s per-language table (arXiv 2402.19173, Table 18) shows e.g. StarCoderBase-3B at Code-ES/ID-F1 of 69.5/62.6 (Python) and 66.4/59.8 (Java) but only 41.4/35.3 (TypeScript); StarCoder2’s authors conclude the “disparity calls for future research on building models that can achieve high performance across diverse languages.” The best multilingual signals are **M2RC-EVAL** (arXiv 2410.21157, 18 languages, ACL 2025, with tree-sitter AST-depth and 11-category semantic annotations) and **CoLA/aiXcoder-7B-v2** (arXiv 2503.15301), trained on Python/Java/C++/Go via SCIP dependency graphs and shown to *generalize to unseen* TypeScript (EM +19.17%) and C# (EM +20.64%) on CrossCodeEval — but per-language navigation-technique ablations for Go/Rust/C/C++ and for front-end framework structure (JSX/TSX, Angular templates + DI) are essentially absent. AST/symbol/graph methods depend on build configuration and type resolution in these languages, so Python-derived gains may not transfer.
- **Incremental indexing / staleness is solved in industry (Glean) but rarely studied academically** as it affects LLM-navigation accuracy.
- **Cost/latency/token economics are reported unevenly** — strong for Agentless ($/issue), LocAgent (−86% cost), and Sourcegraph (token comparisons, vendor), sparse elsewhere.
- **Git-derived coupling and architecture/UML recovery lack rigorous LLM-navigation evaluation** in 2024–2026; promising but unverified.
- **Front-end framework specifics (React/Angular)** have no dedicated navigation-technique evidence; treat as an open risk for any in-house tool.

## Recommendations

**Stage 0 — Adopt, don’t build, the precise-navigation backbone (now).** Stand up SCIP-based indexing (Sourcegraph or open SCIP indexers) or evaluate Glean for your monorepo(s). These already cover TS/JS, Python, Go, Java, Rust, C/C++, give compiler-accurate cross-repo navigation, and have an incremental-indexing story (Glean indexes changes in O(changes)). Expose them to agents via MCP (go_to_definition/find_references/search). This is the highest-confidence, lowest-risk move and directly addresses cross-repo.

**Stage 1 — Default agents to agentic search + precise nav, not vector RAG (now).** Make grep/glob/LSP/SCIP tools the primary navigation path (matches Claude Code/Cursor/Sourcegraph production practice and CodeScaleBench’s observed agent behavior). Avoid investing first in a vector index; if you add embeddings, scope them as a *fallback* for conceptual/NL queries and huge-repo exploration only.

**Stage 2 — Add a repo code graph + hierarchical localization for fault localization and change-impact (next quarter).** Pilot a RepoGraph/LocAgent-style graph layer for localization-heavy workflows; A/B it against pure agentic search on your own tasks. Benchmark to beat: does the graph layer improve localization precision/recall enough to justify build cost?

**Stage 3 — Treat steering files, long-context, and autonomous memory as opt-in, evidence-gated (ongoing).** Keep AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md minimal, human-written, tooling-focused; do NOT auto-generate them. Don’t rely on long-context to replace retrieval. Pilot agentic memory only with reliable selection and measure it explicitly.

**Stage 4 — Commission the cross-repo follow-up** (scoped above), and a language-generalization eval for Go/Rust/C/C++ and React/Angular front-ends, since the published evidence is Python-skewed.

**Thresholds that change the plan:** (a) If an internal A/B shows the graph layer doesn’t beat agentic-search localization on your repos, don’t build/maintain it. (b) If precise-index incrementality can’t keep pace with your commit velocity for C/C++ (Bazel coupling), fall back to agentic search + search-based nav for those languages. (c) If token cost of agentic search at scale exceeds index-build+maintenance cost (measure both), shift more load to precise indexes/semantic fallback. (d) If a future benchmark shows long-context models closing the retrieval gap at acceptable cost on multi-repo tasks, revisit Stage 1.

## Caveats

- **Most effectiveness claims are BENCHMARK, not DEPLOYED.** RepoGraph, LocAgent, CGM, RANGER, RepoCoder, Agentless are benchmark-validated (mostly SWE-bench/RepoEval/CrossCodeEval). Production-validated claims (Claude Code agentic search, Glean, SCIP, Sourcegraph token figures, Copilot memory A/B) are largely vendor-reported or anecdotal — directionally useful, not independently verified.
- **SWE-bench Lite/Verified are near-saturated and partially memorizable;** single-benchmark deltas should not be over-read. AGENTBENCH and SWE-rebench exist to mitigate contamination.
- **Vendor sources (Sourcegraph, Milvus, Cursor, Anthropic) have commercial incentives;** their numbers are flagged as DEPLOYED/vendor throughout, and CodeScaleBench’s per-task-type figures contain an internal inconsistency (noted above) that should be reproduced before relying on it.
- **Language skew:** treat all “effective” verdicts as established for Python (and often Java); generalization to Go/Rust/C/C++ and to React/Angular front-end structure is plausible but under-evidenced and a primary risk for in-house tooling.
- **CGM ablation magnitudes** for the graph-attention component are in the appendix and not extracted here; the qualitative “essential” claim is reported, exact deltas are not.
